histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: Name the three main layers of the skin.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Epidermis (keratinised stratified squamous epithelium), dermis (connective tissue) and hypodermis (subcutaneous fat).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: List the epidermal layers from base to surface.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Stratum basale → stratum spinosum → stratum granulosum → stratum lucidum (thick skin only) → stratum corneum.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: Which epidermal layer contains the dividing stem cells, and which cells accompany them there?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: The stratum basale; it also contains melanocytes and Merkel cells.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: Where is the stratum lucidum found?
What are the three main non-keratinocyte cells of the epidermis and their roles?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Melanocytes (produce melanin, basal layer), Langerhans cells (antigen presentation, stratum spinosum) and Merkel cells (touch reception, basal layer).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What are the two layers of the dermis?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: The papillary dermis (loose connective tissue with dermal papillae) and the reticular dermis (dense irregular connective tissue).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: Name two dermal sensory receptors and what they detect.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Meissner's corpuscles (light touch, in dermal papillae) and Pacinian corpuscles (deep pressure/vibration, deep dermis/hypodermis).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What does the hypodermis contain and do?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Subcutaneous adipose and loose connective tissue; it provides insulation, energy storage and cushioning.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: Name the three main skin cancers and their cell of origin.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Basal cell carcinoma (basal keratinocytes), squamous cell carcinoma (keratinocytes, with keratin pearls) and melanoma (melanocytes).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: How do pemphigus and pemphigoid differ?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Pemphigus targets desmosomes → intra-epidermal blisters; bullous pemphigoid targets hemidesmosomes → sub-epidermal blisters.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What three structures make up the pilosebaceous unit?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: The hair follicle, its sebaceous gland, and the arrector pili muscle.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: Where does hair growth originate in the follicle?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: From the matrix (germinal) cells in the hair bulb, surrounding a vascular dermal papilla.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: By what mechanism do sebaceous glands secrete, and what do they produce?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: By holocrine secretion (the entire cell disintegrates to release its product) — producing sebum, an oily substance.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is the arrector pili muscle and its functions?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: A small smooth muscle attached to the follicle that erects the hair ('goosebumps') and helps express sebum.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is the pathogenesis of acne vulgaris?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Follicular plugging with keratin and sebum, colonisation by Cutibacterium (Propionibacterium) acnes, and inflammation of the pilosebaceous unit.
A cyst formed when a follicle/gland is blocked, filling with keratin/sebum.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What are the two types of sweat gland and where is each found?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Eccrine glands (over the whole body, richest on palms/soles/forehead) and apocrine glands (axilla, groin, areola).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: Where does an eccrine gland open, and what is its function?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Directly onto the skin surface via its own pore; it produces watery sweat for thermoregulation.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: Where does an apocrine gland open, and when does it become active?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Into a hair follicle; it becomes active at puberty and its secretion produces body odour when acted on by skin bacteria.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What cells surround the secretory coil of sweat glands and what do they do?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Myoepithelial cells, which contract to expel the secretion.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What does the eccrine duct do to the sweat?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: It reabsorbs sodium (and chloride), making the final sweat hypotonic.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: How does cystic fibrosis affect sweat, and how is this used diagnostically?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: A CFTR defect prevents chloride (and sodium) reabsorption in the duct, producing abnormally salty sweat — the basis of the sweat test.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: Name the three coats of the eye and their components.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: Outer fibrous (sclera + cornea), middle vascular/uvea (choroid, ciliary body, iris) and inner neural (retina).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: Why is the cornea transparent, and how does it stay dehydrated?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: It is avascular with regularly arranged stromal collagen; its endothelium actively pumps water out to keep it clear.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: List the corneal layers from outside in.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: Epithelium (stratified squamous) → Bowman's membrane → stroma → Descemet's membrane → endothelium.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: What is the lens made of and how does it change shape?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: Transparent crystallin-filled lens fibres within a capsule, suspended by zonules from the ciliary body, which alter its curvature for accommodation.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: Trace the flow of visual signals through the retina.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: Light passes through the inner retina to the photoreceptors (rods and cones) at the back → bipolar cells → ganglion cells, whose axons form the optic nerve.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: What are the fovea and the optic disc?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: The fovea (cone-rich) gives the sharpest vision; the optic disc is where axons leave and vessels enter — the blind spot (no photoreceptors).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: What is the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: A pigmented cell layer behind the photoreceptors that supports them (phagocytoses shed discs, absorbs stray light).
Opacification of the lens (from crystallin protein changes), causing painless progressive visual loss.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: What is the function of the cochlea?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: To convert sound vibrations into electrical nerve signals (auditory transduction).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: Name the three ducts of the cochlea and their fluid.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: Scala vestibuli and scala tympani (containing perilymph) and the scala media/cochlear duct (containing endolymph).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: What is the organ of Corti and where does it sit?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: The sensory receptor organ of hearing, sitting on the basilar membrane within the cochlear duct.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: How do hair cells transduce sound?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: Sound vibrates the basilar membrane, bending the stereocilia (which touch the tectorial membrane); this opens ion channels and depolarises the hair cells, activating the cochlear nerve.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: What is tonotopy in the cochlea?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: Different sound frequencies stimulate different regions of the basilar membrane — the base responds to high frequencies and the apex to low frequencies.
Loss or damage of the cochlear hair cells (from noise, ageing/presbycusis or ototoxic drugs) or the cochlear nerve.
Endolymphatic hydrops (excess endolymph) causing episodic vertigo, tinnitus and fluctuating hearing loss.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: Where is olfactory epithelium located and what type of epithelium is it?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: In the roof of the nasal cavity; it is a tall pseudostratified epithelium.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: Name the three cell types of olfactory epithelium.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: Olfactory (bipolar) sensory neurons, supporting (sustentacular) cells and basal (stem) cells.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: What is special about olfactory receptor neurons?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: They are bipolar neurons whose cilia bind odorants and whose axons form cranial nerve I (olfactory nerve); they can regenerate from basal cells.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: What is the role of Bowman's glands in the nose?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: They secrete a serous fluid that dissolves odorant molecules so they can be detected.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: Where are taste buds located and what is their shape?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: In the epithelium of the tongue papillae (fungiform, foliate, circumvallate); they are barrel-shaped clusters of cells.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: What cells make up a taste bud and how do tastants reach them?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: Gustatory (receptor) cells, supporting cells and basal cells; tastants enter through a taste pore at the surface.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: What five taste modalities are detected, and by which nerves?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: Sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami; innervated by cranial nerves VII, IX and X.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: The correct order of epidermal layers from deep to superficial is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: From base to surface: stratum basale → spinosum → granulosum → lucidum (thick skin only) → corneum.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: The stratum lucidum is found only in:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: The clear stratum lucidum is present only in thick, hairless skin of the palms and soles.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Which epidermal cell produces the pigment melanin?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Melanocytes in the stratum basale synthesise melanin and transfer it to surrounding keratinocytes.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Light touch in the dermal papillae is detected by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Meissner's corpuscles in the dermal papillae detect light touch; Pacinian corpuscles in the deep dermis detect pressure/vibration.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Keratin pearls in a skin tumour are characteristic of:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma shows keratinisation with keratin pearls; melanoma is S100-positive and BCC shows basaloid nests with peripheral palisading.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Sebaceous glands secrete sebum by which mechanism?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Sebaceous glands use holocrine secretion — the entire cell breaks down to release sebum into the hair follicle.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: The pilosebaceous unit consists of the hair follicle, sebaceous gland and:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: The arrector pili (smooth) muscle completes the pilosebaceous unit and erects the hair.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Hair is produced by the matrix cells located in the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Matrix (germinal) cells in the hair bulb proliferate around the vascular dermal papilla to grow the hair shaft.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Eccrine sweat glands function primarily in:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Eccrine glands secrete watery sweat onto the skin surface for evaporative cooling (thermoregulation).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Apocrine sweat glands open into:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Apocrine glands (axilla, groin, areola) empty into hair follicles and become active at puberty.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Abnormally salty sweat used as a diagnostic test is characteristic of:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: In cystic fibrosis a CFTR defect prevents chloride/sodium reabsorption by the sweat duct, giving salty sweat (the sweat test).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: The cornea remains transparent partly because its ______ pumps water out of the stroma.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: The corneal endothelium actively pumps water out of the stroma to keep it dehydrated and clear; the cornea is also avascular.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: In the retina, light must pass through the inner layers to reach the ______ at the back.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: The photoreceptors (rods and cones) lie at the back of the neural retina; signals then pass to bipolar cells and ganglion cells whose axons form the optic nerve.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: The region of sharpest visual acuity, rich in cones, is the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: The fovea (in the macula) is packed with cones and provides the highest acuity; the optic disc is the blind spot.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: Opacification of the lens causing painless visual loss is a:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: A cataract is lens opacification (crystallin protein change), giving gradual painless visual loss.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: The sensory receptor cells of hearing, located in the organ of Corti, are the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: Hair cells with apical stereocilia in the organ of Corti transduce basilar-membrane vibration into nerve signals.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: The organ of Corti rests on the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: The organ of Corti sits on the basilar membrane; the stereocilia of its hair cells contact the overlying tectorial membrane.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: Which cochlear duct contains endolymph?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: The scala media (cochlear duct) contains endolymph; the scala vestibuli and scala tympani contain perilymph.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: Loss of cochlear hair cells from noise or ageing causes:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: Damage to the sensory hair cells (or cochlear nerve) causes sensorineural hearing loss (e.g. noise-induced, presbycusis, ototoxicity).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: The receptor cells of the olfactory epithelium are:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: Olfactory receptors are bipolar neurons whose cilia bind odorants and whose axons form the olfactory nerve (CN I); notably they can regenerate.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: Olfactory epithelium is classified as:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: Olfactory epithelium is a tall pseudostratified epithelium containing bipolar neurons, supporting cells and basal cells.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: Taste buds are found within the epithelium of the tongue's:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: Taste buds are barrel-shaped receptor clusters located in the fungiform, foliate and circumvallate papillae, opening via a taste pore.
